explanations.answer: Smash the pillars and tear down the high places
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. They broke up the sacred pillars, chopped down the Asherah poles, and tore down the high places and altars. The text says they kept at it "until they had utterly destroyed them all." They took the job seriously, and that's a whole lot of demolition after a worship service.

explanations.answer: Build new altars on every hilltop
explanations.explanation: It's the other direction, friend. These Israelites came from worshiping in Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah they tore down altars. They tore down the high places too. Nobody picked up a hammer to build anything new in this verse.

explanations.answer: Read the Law aloud at every city gate
explanations.explanation: Good thought, but this verse doesn't say that. What it says is that they broke up the sacred pillars, chopped down the Asherah poles, and tore down the high places and altars. It was a big cleanup. I'd bring a lot of work gloves to that one.

True, baker. The verse says they tore these things down throughout Judah and Benjamin, "as well as in Ephraim and Manasseh." Four regions, one job, and the text says they didn't quit until it was all destroyed. That's a lot of ground to cover.

It's true, friend. The verse says they tore these things down throughout Judah and Benjamin, "as well as in Ephraim and Manasseh." It doesn't stop at the first two names on the list. The work covered all four regions.

Yes, baker. Hezekiah, king of Judah, set the divisions back up for the burnt offerings and peace offerings, for ministry, for giving thanks, and for singing praises at the gates of the LORD's dwelling. So praise was part of the job description. Honestly, that's a better list than most of us have at work.

Not on this list, friend. The verse names burnt offerings, peace offerings, ministry, giving thanks and singing praises at the gates of the LORD's dwelling. Everything on it centers on the LORD's house. The palace isn't mentioned.

Tax collecting isn't in this verse, baker. The duties named are the burnt offerings and peace offerings, ministry, giving thanks, and singing praises at the gates of the LORD's dwelling. That's the whole list. Nobody's knocking on doors with a clipboard.

explanations.answer: The king from his own possessions
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The text says the king contributed from his own possessions for the regular morning and evening burnt offerings, and for the Sabbaths, New Moons and appointed feasts. That was Hezekiah's own money, not a bill passed to somebody else. It was all done as written in the Law of the LORD.

explanations.answer: The priests from their own flocks
explanations.explanation: Close, but the verse names someone else. It says the king contributed from his own possessions for these offerings. The priests are the ones serving. Hezekiah is the one paying.

explanations.answer: The officials from the city treasury
explanations.explanation: No treasury shows up in this verse, friend. It says "The king contributed from his own possessions." Hezekiah reached into his own pocket for the morning and evening offerings, the Sabbaths, the New Moons and the feasts.

explanations.answer: So they can devote themselves to the Law of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Hezekiah commanded the people in Jerusalem to make a contribution so the priests and Levites "could devote themselves to the Law of the LORD." The gift is there so they can give themselves to that work. I like that. It's like keeping the oven stocked so the baker can stay focused on the baking.

explanations.answer: So they can repair the house of the LORD
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but this verse gives a different reason. The contribution is for the priests and Levites, "so that they could devote themselves to the Law of the LORD." Repairs aren't mentioned here. The giving was about freeing them up for the Law.

explanations.answer: So they can rebuild the walls of Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: No walls in this verse, friend. Hezekiah commands the people living in Jerusalem to make a contribution for the priests and Levites. The reason given is "so that they could devote themselves to the Law of the LORD." That's the whole purpose the text gives.

Generously is the word, baker. The Israelites "generously provided the firstfruits of the grain, new wine, oil, and honey." Verse 5 adds that they brought in an abundance, a tithe of everything. I'd love to see that line at the front door.

That's not the word the text uses, friend. It says the Israelites "generously provided" the firstfruits. Nothing there suggests dragging their feet. They brought in an abundance, a tithe of everything.

Nothing sneaky going on here, baker. The text says the Israelites "generously provided" the firstfruits of the grain, new wine, oil and honey. And you can't give in secret and also bring in an abundance. A tithe of everything is hard to hide.

Not quite, baker. The order went to the people in Jerusalem, but verse 6 says the Israelites and Judahites who lived in the cities of Judah "also brought a tithe." So the giving spread past the capital. Jerusalem wasn't carrying this alone.

Yes, it's false. Verse 6 says the Israelites and Judahites living in the cities of Judah also brought a tithe of their herds and flocks. They brought a tithe of the holy things consecrated to the LORD their God too. So the giving reached well past Jerusalem.

Seventh month, baker. The text says they began building up the heaps in the third month and finished in the seventh. That's four months of bringing and stacking. I've waited that long for a pan of cookies to cool when I wasn't paying attention.
Not the fourth, friend. The text says they began in the third month and finished in the seventh. So it ran well past the fourth. They kept stacking.
That's too far out, baker. The text says they began building up the heaps in the third month and finished in the seventh. They were done by the seventh month. They never made it to a twelfth.

explanations.answer: They bless the LORD and His people Israel
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Hezekiah and his officials viewed the heaps, and they blessed the LORD and His people Israel. They blessed God and they blessed the people who brought the gifts. A pile that big deserves a big thank-you.

explanations.answer: They count each heap and write it down
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't show any counting, friend. It says that when Hezekiah and his officials came and viewed the heaps, they blessed the LORD and His people Israel. Their first response was blessing.

explanations.answer: They order the gifts sent to the palace
explanations.explanation: No palace in this verse, baker. Hezekiah and his officials came and viewed the heaps, and they blessed the LORD and His people Israel. Later he commands storerooms to be prepared in the house of the LORD.

explanations.answer: The LORD has blessed His people
explanations.explanation: That's what he says, baker. Azariah, the chief priest of the household of Zadok, tells Hezekiah they've had enough to eat with plenty left over, "…because the LORD has blessed His people…" That's the reason he gives. He points to the LORD.

explanations.answer: The land has yielded a double harvest
explanations.explanation: Azariah doesn't say that, friend. Azariah, the chief priest, says they have had enough to eat since the people began to bring their contributions. His reason is "…the LORD has blessed His people…" He never mentions a harvest number.

explanations.answer: The priests have kept back their portions
explanations.explanation: That's not what Azariah says, baker. Azariah, the chief priest of the household of Zadok, says it began when the people started to bring their contributions into the house of the LORD. His reason is "…the LORD has blessed His people…" No one is hiding anything.

Storerooms, baker. Hezekiah commanded them to prepare storerooms in the house of the LORD, and they did so. When you've got heaps that big, you need somewhere to put them. I once ran out of cooling racks, so I understand the pressure.
Not altars, friend. Hezekiah commanded them to prepare storerooms in the house of the LORD. After all those heaps, the gifts needed a place to be kept. The text says they did so.

Not courtyards, baker. The verse says Hezekiah commanded them to prepare storerooms in the house of the LORD. The gifts needed space inside. Verse 12 says they faithfully brought in the contributions, tithes and dedicated gifts.

explanations.answer: He did what was good and upright and true
explanations.explanation: That's the summary, baker. The writer says, "He did what was good and upright and true before the LORD his God." That's one sentence summing up everything he did throughout Judah. Honestly, I'd take that written on my apron.

explanations.answer: He did what the priests told him to do
explanations.explanation: That's not how the writer sums it up, friend. The text says Hezekiah "did what was good and upright and true before the LORD his God." The priests aren't named in that line. It's all about Hezekiah before the LORD.

explanations.answer: He did what his officials thought best
explanations.explanation: Not quite, baker. The writer says Hezekiah "did what was good and upright and true before the LORD his God." His officials aren't part of that sentence. The line is about Hezekiah and the LORD.

True, baker. The text says Hezekiah "acted with all his heart in every work that he began in the service of the house of God." All his heart, every work. I can't even finish one batch without sneaking a bite.

It's actually true, friend. The text says Hezekiah "acted with all his heart in every work that he began in the service of the house of God." That covers the law and the commandments too. He did it in order to seek his God.
He prospers, baker. The text says he acted with all his heart "in order to seek his God. And so he prospered." That's the outcome it gives. I'll leave it right there.
Good word, but it isn't the one the text uses. It says Hezekiah acted with all his heart in order to seek his God, "And so he prospered." Wisdom isn't mentioned. The outcome named is prosperity.

Not in this verse, friend. The text says he acted with all his heart in order to seek his God, "And so he prospered." Nothing here mentions how long he lived. The result it gives is that he prospered.
